data.text/markdown:
Your First xG Model

A hands-on NHSSAA lesson: teach a computer to grade soccer shots Inspired by Chris Dove's NHSSAA Summer Symposium webinar (June 2026). All code in this notebook is original, written for the NHSSAA community. xG (expected goals) is the number you hear on TV: "that shot was 0.35 xG." It means: shots like this one go in about 35% of the time. Today you will build that number yourself, from 8,000+ real Bundesliga shots, one clue at a time. No install needed: press Run and everything happens right here in your browser.

Step 0 - Get the data

We use Impect Open Data: every event of the 2023/24 Bundesliga season, free for learning and research. The notebook downloads match files straight from Impect's public repository - by using them you agree to the Impect open-data terms. A Bundesliga season has 34 matchdays (9 games each). Loading more matchdays gives the model more shots to learn from, but takes longer:
  • In the browser: keep it small (1-3 matchdays). Each matchday is ~50 MB.
  • On your own computer: crank it to 34 for all ~8,069 shots.

data.text/markdown: Loaded 498 shots from 18 matches.

Step 1 - Meet a shot

Every shot in the data answers a few simple questions:
question field in the data
where was the shooter? start.adjCoordinates (x, y in meters)
foot or head? bodyPart
was it a penalty? action == "PENALTY_KICK"
did it go in? result == "SUCCESS"
Coordinates are in meters, with the center circle at (0, 0) and the goal the shooter attacks at (52.5, 0). From x and y we can compute the two most famous clues in shot analysis:
  • distance - how far from the goal?
  • angle - how much of the goal can the shooter see?

data.text/markdown:
Clue 1 - Distance

Guess first: does distance matter? Let's let the data answer. We bucket shots by how far out they were and count how often each bucket scored.

data.text/markdown:
Clue 2 - Angle

Two shots from the same distance are not equal: one in front of goal, one near the sideline. The difference is how much of the goal mouth the shooter can see - the angle. Look at the map below: color = how often shots from that spot scored. Distance alone can't draw this picture.

Clue 3 - Head or foot?

Headers are harder: the ball comes in the air, you have less control. Same distance, very different story.

data.text/markdown:
Clue 4 - Penalties break the pattern

A penalty is always from the same spot, with no defender in the way. No model of "normal" shots can price it - so analysts hard-code it. Historically about 76% of penalties are scored, so xG models just say:
penalty = 0.76 xG, always.
Check the data yourself below - how close is this season to 0.76?

Step 3 - Does each clue actually help?

Time to be scientists. We train tiny models that each see one more clue than the last, and measure the error with log loss (lower = better at putting high numbers on real goals and low numbers on misses).
  1. No clues - predict the same average for every shot
  2. + distance
  3. + angle
  4. + header?
  5. penalties handled by the hard-coded 0.76

data.text/markdown:
Step 4 - The real model: gradient-boosted trees

Pros don't stop at straight-line rules. LightGBM (a gradient-boosted trees model - the kind used at real clubs) learns curves and combinations on its own: how distance matters differently at big angles, how headers change everything, and so on. Below we train it on all non-penalty shots, then glue the two pieces together:
  • normal shots: the model's prediction
  • penalties: the hard-coded 0.76
A fair warning from real life: with only three clues, the simple models above are already very good, and the fancy model only matches them. Boosted trees earn their keep when you feed them more clues - that is exactly what the challenges at the end ask you to do.

Step 5 - Draw the model's brain

Let's ask the model "what if?" for every spot on the pitch and paint the answers. This is the map TV analysts show when they talk about "good shooting positions".

Step 6 - Your turn

Build a shot. Move the sliders and watch the model grade it.

Your shot: 0.18 xG

Out of 100 shots like yours, about 18 would go in. For comparison, an average shot in this dataset scores 13 times out of 100.

Keep going (challenges)

  1. Left foot, right foot? Add bodyPart == "FOOT_LEFT" as a clue. Does it help or just add noise?
  2. Find the flukes. Which goals had xG under 0.05? Find one on YouTube and decide: lucky, or is the model missing a clue?
  3. Best finishers. Join the shots to the players file and ask: who scores more than their xG says they should?
  4. Break it. Train on the first half of the season, test on the second. Does the model still work on matches it has never seen?
